paras: The threatened lynching of Frank Dodge took place at Peach Springs, Arizona Territory, on 7 August 1888, when residents prepared to hang Dodge, a railroad section foreman, after he was accused of assaulting the young daughter of a train conductor. The party gave up the plan and let the law take its course, and Dodge was later indicted for rape in Mohave County. Arizona and California papers carried the story, and one Flagstaff paper at first printed the names of the accused and the father reversed.

Dodge, about forty-five, had worked for the Atlantic & Pacific railroad for several years, but according to the Mohave County Miner drink had cost him his positions. The Flagstaff Champion later described him as living in a hut at Peach Springs at the time. A wire dispatch from Needles said he had come from Coolidge, New Mexico, "where, it is said," he had committed a similar crime.

On the afternoon of Monday, 6 August, Dodge was arrested on the accusation of assaulting the seven- or eight-year-old daughter of Conductor Samuel Cunningham. By the child's account, as the Miner gave it, Dodge coaxed her into his cabin with a promise of peaches and tried but failed to assault her, and she told her mother. The Needles dispatch reported that the officers holding Dodge were feared unable to protect him "from the vengeance of the indignant citizens."

Early on the morning of 7 August, according to a dispatch from Peach Springs, an "avenging party" prepared a rope and selected a telegraph pole on which to hang Dodge. The same dispatch said that "by cool counsel" the party agreed to let the law take its course, and the Miner likewise wrote that the excitement was "by better counsel allayed."

District Attorney Eb. Williams, Under Sheriff Kuencer and Deputy Maynard came to Peach Springs for an examination on Tuesday before Justice of the Peace Mollering. Dodge was held to answer with bail set at $4,000 and, unable to pay it, was taken to the jail at Kingman. At the September term of the district court a grand jury indicted him for rape, and the case was continued to the next term with bail again at $4,000. Cunningham, his wife and his daughter attended the court as witnesses, but no report of a trial verdict was found.

The Arizona Weekly Journal-Miner ran the Peach Springs dispatch under the headline "Hanging too Good for Him," called Dodge "the fiend," and repeated a report that this was his third such offense. In California the Sacramento Daily Record-Union carried the Associated Press version as "A BRUTE" with the subhead "Indignant Citizens Threaten to Lynch a Rape Flend." The Tombstone Epitaph condensed the dispatch into its Arizona news column, while the Clifton Clarion printed a single line about the arrest of "C. T. Dodge" with no mention of a lynching.

The Mohave County Miner, the county paper, gave the fullest account, called the offense an "attempt at rape," and a week later noted that Dodge had been promoted for bravery in an Ohio regiment during the war. None of the papers mentioned the race of anyone involved.

The Flagstaff Champion first reported that Cunningham had been arrested for raping Dodge's daughter and that a lynching attempt on him had been frustrated. The Mohave County Miner replied that "the true statement is exactly the reverse," and the Champion printed a correction saying railroad men had mixed up the names. An uncorrected copy of the reversed version still appeared in the St. Johns Herald on 23 August, credited to the Miner.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Dodge
bases: A party prepared a rope and chose a telegraph pole to hang Dodge, a prisoner accused of rape, but no one was killed (A3, A5); the episode is a threatened lynching.

Dodge was not killed; the 'avenging party' agreed to let the law take its course (A3, A4), so the definition's killing element is absent although a lynching was planned in response to a rape accusation.
A wire dispatch (A2), a Peach Springs dispatch (A3) and the county paper's own report (A4) agree that Dodge was arrested on a rape accusation and was threatened with lynching; A5 repeats A3.

accounts.label: Peach Springs dispatch
accounts.gist: Dodge committed rape on Cunningham's seven-year-old child; a party prepared a rope and picked a telegraph pole early next morning but agreed to let the law take its course.

accounts.label: California Associated Press wire (Needles)
accounts.gist: Dodge 'brutally assaulted' the girl and was in officers' custody, but it was feared they could not protect him from indignant citizens.

accounts.label: Mohave County Miner (local)
accounts.gist: An 'attempt at rape' that failed, by the child's own story; feeling ran high enough to fear a lynching until better counsel prevailed; Dodge examined and jailed at Kingman.

accounts.label: Flagstaff Champion (first version)
accounts.gist: Cunningham was arrested for raping Dodge's daughter and a lynching attempt on him was frustrated; later retracted.

framing.detail: The Journal-Miner headed the dispatch 'Hanging too Good for Him' and called Dodge 'the fiend' while reporting approvingly that 'cool counsel' prevailed.
The Sacramento Record-Union ran the wire as 'A BRUTE. Indignant Citizens Threaten to Lynch a Rape Flend.'
The Mohave County Miner reported the case as an 'attempt at rape' and credited 'better counsel' with letting the law take its course; it also corrected the Champion's reversed names.
